[MUQATIL:101:1-6/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Heavy scales belong to those whose good deeds outweigh their evil deeds.

[TAB-FULL:v24p594#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says there is no actual scale; the scale is a metaphor.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p327#2/r13] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the scales mean the account, as illustrated by calling the human tongue their measure and by a poem about the measure.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p328/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · عبد العزيز بن يحيى | reports | Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya says the scales are proofs and arguments, citing the same poem as evidence.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p328/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Mawardi says موازين may be a plural of ميزان, or a plural meaning weighed things.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p264/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | Muqatil similarly says the truth is heavy and falsehood is light.
[WAHIDI-QT:101:6/r1] WAHIDI-QT, d. 468 · author | holds | His scales are heavy with good deeds.

[IBNATIYYA:101:6/r3] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | The plural balances are assigned to a person because that person has many different things to be weighed.
[IBNATIYYA:101:6/r4] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | A balance is heavy through faith and deeds, and light through their absence or scarcity; a believer’s balance will never be disastrously light.
[TABRISI:101:5-11/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Heavy scales mean abundant good deeds and many acts of goodness.

[RAZI:101:6/r5] RAZI, d. 606 · المتكلمون | reports | The theologians say deeds themselves cannot be weighed, especially after ceasing to exist; instead, records may be weighed, light and darkness may signify good and evil, or the records may be embodied beautifully or hideously, publicly revealing people's standing.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p70/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farraʾ takes موازين as weighed deeds, meaning actions that have weight and consequence with God.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p70/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbas takes موازين as scales with a tongue and two pans; good deeds appear beautiful and outweigh, while the unbeliever's ugly deeds are light.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p70/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says the scale has two pans but its nature is not described.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p70/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المتكلمون | reports | Theologians say past good and bad acts cannot themselves be weighed; instead, written records, light and darkness, or beautiful and ugly forms of records display their weight.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p70/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The weighing publicly reveals the righteous person's state and increases joy, while exposing the evildoer to humiliation before all creatures.
[QURTUBI:101:6/r1] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | The author refers readers to earlier discussions of the balance in al-Aʿrāf, al-Kahf, and al-Anbiyāʾ, and in his book al-Tadhkira. | mentions 7:8, 18:105, 21:47
[QURTUBI:101:6/r2] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | The balance has a pan and a tongue, and weighs written records of good and bad deeds.
[QURTUBI:101:6/r3] QURTUBI, d. 671 · قيل | reports | One view says a single balance held by Gabriel weighs human deeds, expressed in the plural; a poem also uses plural balances.
[QURTUBI:101:6/r4] QURTUBI, d. 671 · author | holds | The author cites poetic usage of the plural balances for separate events.
[QURTUBI:101:6/r5] QURTUBI, d. 671 · عبد العزيز بن يحيى | reports | Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya says the balances are proofs and arguments, citing a poet who calls the argument of each disputant his balance.
[BAYDAWI:101:6/r1] BAYDAWI, d. 685 · author | holds | His scales are heavy because the measures of the kinds of his good deeds outweigh.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:101:1-11/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Heavy scales mean the total weight of kinds of good deeds prevails.
[NASAFI:101:6/r1] NASAFI, d. 710 · author | holds | The scales weigh heavily because their owners followed the truth.

[ALUSI:101:6/r5] ALUSI, d. 1270 · ابن عباس والحسن البصري | reports | A tangible balance is transmitted from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan al-Basri and attributed to many commentators by Sharh al-Maqasid.
[ALUSI:101:6/r6] ALUSI, d. 1270 · نوادر الأصول | reports | Nawadir al-Usul locates the balance between Paradise and Hell and describes its attachment to the Throne, with Gabriel holding its column and Michael overseeing it.
[ALUSI:101:6/r7] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | prefers | The best-known and sounder view is one balance for all communities and all deeds.
[ALUSI:101:6/r8] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Mawāzīn is the plural of mīzān; its original wāw becomes yāʾ because it is quiescent after a kasra.
